previous.passage: By the time you read this, Grandpa Lachlan, the water in the Havana cellar will have gone down, or so the neighbors promise. I waded in this morning to find your Gaelic word cards floating like little rafts, the ink on the S's running blue. For an hour I could only stand there and count the ruined ones. Then I remembered how you made me repeat your goodnight phrase every evening until I stopped stumbling, and I began lifting the cards out one by one and pegging them on the line across the patio. Many can still be read. I am copying each onto fresh paper, and I have learned eleven new words already, though I am sure I say half of them wrong. Your Ximena. Señora Ruiz from upstairs has lent me her fan to dry them.

options: Dismayed, dwelling on the ruined cards in the flooded cellar
Discouraged, with only a slight hint of determination
Determined and hopeful, after a moment of dismay
Bitter toward the neighbors for their empty promises

previous.passage: We had not spoken in four years, Greta and I, not since she lured my best customer across the square with her poppy-seed rolls. So when the stationmaster told us that the new café at the Hamburg terminal would have only one table for pastries, and that we must share it, I, Annika, nearly refused. On the first morning she set her rolls on the left and I set my almond cakes on the right, and neither of us looked up. By noon, though, I noticed she had moved her tray an inch to give my cakes the light from the window. Before closing, I tasted one of her rolls in the stockroom; it was better than mine, and I told her so the next day. She only sniffed and said my almonds were too dry. A train from Altona hissed to a stop beyond the glass.

Annika admires Greta, who has come to rely on Annika's baking judgment.
They are old friends who quarrel only to amuse the café's customers.
They are rivals who are beginning to show each other a wary respect.

previous.passage: Years later, I still remember the frost on the guesthouse windows the morning Aunt Itzel and I had to decide which of us would stay. We owed the brothers for a whole winter of lodging on the plateau, and the abbot had agreed that one of us could work it off through spring while the other drove home to Flagstaff. I, Nova, said I would stay; I was nineteen and strong, and she had a job waiting. Itzel only poured me coffee and slid the truck keys across the table toward my hand. When I pushed them back, she closed my fingers around them and said that she had stayed behind for my mother once, too, and had never regretted it. I left at noon. Snow was drifting against the mesa's red flank as I passed the cattle guard.
previous.question: Which choice best describes the relationship between Itzel and Nova as presented in the text?
options: Itzel insists on sacrificing for Nova, who wants to bear the burden herself.
Nova resents Itzel for forcing her to leave the plateau guesthouse before spring.
Itzel depends on Nova, who reluctantly agrees to stay behind and work.
They are distant relatives bound together mainly by the debt they share.

previous.passage: When the looms of the Tbilisi weaving cooperative fall silent each evening, I set two chairs by the window, and Anushka begins unwinding the tangled yarn the weavers leave behind. We used to play here for them on Fridays; now nobody asks. IRENA: You could leave the yarn tonight. ANUSHKA: (without looking up) And give up the only thing we still do on time? Later, when I reach for my violin case, she slides the spool toward me first, as she always does, so that I hold one end while she winds. Neither of us mentions the concert hall that cancelled our booking. IRENA: Same tempo as yesterday? ANUSHKA: Slower. Your hands are tired.
